A Thanksgiving roundup of eight search changes from this year worth a thank-you, from AI visibility data and social reports to a back button policy.

In SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate. Today is a day to consider what we are thankful for, so let us dig deep and create our SEO Thanksgiving list.

Search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility. We can take the crumbs.

This article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC. We finish off with a celebration for anybody who clicked their back button and went somewhere they had never been before.

Google Search Console is currently displaying dedicated reports for your impressions in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and generative AI features in Discover, by page, country, and date. These new reports were released in June, and Google’s announcement now says, “As of August 31, 2026, we’ve rolled out these insights to all websites worldwide.”

We’re glad to finally see the AI impressions separated out from the normal impression totals.

SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide

Microsoft Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI performance report in February as a public preview, showing how many times Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summarizations, and some partner integrations reference your content, along with the referenced pages and the grounding query (the phrase used by the AI to retrieve the content).

In June, Microsoft added a Citation Share feature in preview, which provides insight into what percentage of citations for a grounding query go to your site. The February report gives you a count of how many times you appeared in the citation list, and Citation Share shows how large a piece of the pie those citations represent.

SEJ covered it here: Bing Webmaster Tools Adds AI Citation Performance Data and here Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide

On Nov. 10, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Business Hub in beta. All eligible businesses where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in Business Hub and, after claims and identity verification are approved, will be able to see mentions, website clicks, and discovery topics over the past 28 days.

According to OpenAI’s setup guide for online businesses, a mention occurs when ChatGPT references your website, not if it just names your brand.

Vahan Petrosyan, director of technology for SEJ, submitted Search Engine Journal, and Business Hub showed 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10.

SEJ’s mentions and website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10. Screenshot by Vahan Petrosyan, Search Engine Journal.

This is a beta version, and OpenAI says that claiming a business does not assure greater visibility within ChatGPT. However, these numbers are provided directly from ChatGPT, and mentions cannot be reflected in referral reports.

SEJ covered it here: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub

Google introduced platform properties for social and video accounts in July and made them available to everybody worldwide on July 29. They provide information regarding clicks, impressions, CTR and average position for posts on Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube appearing in Google Search. Reports for Discover and Google News will also be displayed when applicable.

The Insights report for a YouTube platform property shows clicks from Google Search over 28 days. Source: Google Search Central (CC BY 4.0, cropped).

Your social team can now track how users locate the team’s social content on Google Search, within Search Console, the same tool utilized by your SEO team.

SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console Adds Reports For Social Posts

Google announced the branded queries filter last November and made it available to all eligible sites by March. The branded queries filter allows you to sort your Performance report queries into branded, including misspellings, and non-branded, so you can identify traffic coming from users searching specifically for your brand or products.

The Search Analytics API got the same branded split this month. Prior to this branded queries filter being implemented, tracking traffic based upon specific branded searches required “maintaining complex keyword regex lists,” as Google put it. Many will agree that it is refreshing to no longer need such lists.

SEJ covered it here: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API

Google’s September Small Business Bulletin described view counts for Business Profile posts as “currently rolling out globally.”

Once the rollout has completed for your Business Profile, each post card located under the dashboard section will indicate views generated from Search and Maps activity for posts from the past 18 months.

Google removed post metrics from Business Profiles in 2023. Now you can determine which posts receive the most views rather than making educated guesses. However, the bulletin said the counts were not accessible via the API yet.

SEJ covered it here: Google Adds Post View Counts To Business Profiles

For PPC advertisers working in TikTok Ads Manager, the Q4 product preview highlighted Impression Share, a common metric seen in Google Ads, along with Top 1 Impression Share for Search Ads campaigns.

Impression Share measures the percentage of eligible search results impressions that your ads capture. According to TikTok’s help section, availability of Impression Share may vary depending on account and market. Still, it can quickly reveal what portion of eligible search visibility you are leaving behind.

TikTok also added Keyword Packs (pre-made brand and category keywords) to the Keyword Suggestion Tool for a faster way to create keyword lists.

SEJ covered it here: TikTok Search Ads Adds Brand And Category Keyword Packs

Google began treating back button hijacking as a malicious practice in April and started enforcing this policy on June 15. Sites using back button hijacking could be subject to either a manual action or automated demotion.

On Nov. 23, Google released a new FAQ which says the policy will apply if the back button hijacking occurs in a user’s browser, including when they visit your page via social media. Although this policy cannot eliminate all cases of back button hijacking, websites currently utilizing this tactic may want to stop.

SEJ covered it here: Google Says Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits

Our single request for next year’s Thanksgiving holiday is the ability to differentiate Search Console’s AI clicks from web clicks. Currently, every time someone clicks on an AI Overview or AI Mode link, that click counts in the same Performance report as clicks on your other search engine results.

Happy Thanksgiving from all the SEJ team.

From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

The Chicago Sun-Times announced a new slogan this week. What is it?

“Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

“The union has been negotiating a new contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”

A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

“Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”

“It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”

Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

Unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a big increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

YouTube has found a new way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

“YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows.”

In Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government plans to scrap public media license fees.

#7326. The Missing Step In Prompt Tracking Was Written Down In 1995 via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Prompt tracking has no method for choosing prompts or defining a correct answer. Competency questions, a 1995 knowledge engineering method, fill that gap.

The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be. That second problem is older than the first, and it has a documented solution that predates Google. Knowledge engineers have used it since the mid-1990s under the name competency questions, and it is almost absent from the conversation in search.

Over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured quickly. Practitioners now broadly accept that a single run of a single prompt tells you very little, that branded and unbranded prompts have to be reported separately, and that wording changes results. The research supports the caution. A peer-reviewed study presented at ICLR 2024 found that formatting changes alone, with the meaning of the prompt untouched, moved one open-source model’s accuracy by as much as 76 points on standard benchmark tasks. That study tested benchmarks, not brands, but it establishes the underlying behavior: These systems respond to the form of a question as well as its content.

What has not matured is the step before sampling. A scoping review posted this fall examined 38 empirical studies that query language models and measure outcomes for brands, and it judged that only five of them could defend how their prompts were chosen. Most used prompts written by the authors or generated by a model, with no evidence that those prompts represent what buyers ask. A separate survey makes the consequence plain: the prompts you pick, and the weight you give each one, define the market your visibility score describes, and that market may not match real demand. Both papers are preprints from single authors and have not been through peer review, so I treat them as a careful reading of the field and not as final findings.

The same review found that authors with a commercial stake in visibility services, or in a brand being measured, were behind 19 of those 38 studies. I am one of those people, since I founded CitationIQ, which measures AI visibility, and you should weigh what follows with that understanding (I was not part of any of those studies, for the record).

The practical result is familiar to anyone who has sat in a prompt-selection meeting or had to choose them. Someone opens a spreadsheet, the team brainstorms questions, a tool suggests a few hundred more, and the list is frozen so that next month’s number can be compared with this month’s. Nobody writes down why each prompt is there, what business situation it stands for, or what the model would have to say for the answer to count as right. The score that comes out is precise, and its meaning is undefined.

In the early 1990s, Michael Grüninger and Mark Fox at the University of Toronto were building formal models of how enterprises operate, and they needed a way to decide what a model had to contain before anyone built it. Their answer, published in 1995, was to start with the situations the model had to support and then write the questions it must be able to answer in those situations. They called these competency questions because the questions define what the model is competent to do.

The thing they were building is called an ontology, which is easiest to relate to the knowledge graph you already know. The graph holds the facts, and the ontology is the plan those facts are organized by: what kinds of things exist, what properties they carry, and how they can relate. Schema.org plays that role for structured data on the web. Most entity work fills in the graph without stating what it must be able to answer, which is the gap competency questions close. From here on I will call the ontology a knowledge model.

A competency question is a question a knowledge model must be able to answer, written down before the model is built and used afterward to test whether it works. The questions come first, they come from real situations, and they double as the acceptance test. The Toronto method ran in six stages: Describe the motivating scenarios, write the questions informally, define the terms, restate the questions formally, write the rules, and then establish the conditions under which the model answers the questions completely. Later researchers borrowed test-first development from software engineering and turned the questions into tests that are written before the model is changed.

Set that beside the spreadsheet. The knowledge engineer can trace every question to a scenario and every test to a question. The prompt list has no scenarios behind it and no expected answers in front of it.

It would be convenient to say that knowledge engineers solved this and marketers only need to copy them, and it would be wrong. A 2023 survey of 63 ontology engineers found that most of them use competency questions routinely, and that 77.8% have difficulty making sure their questions are both necessary and sufficient. Nearly two-thirds have trouble identifying questions that truly represent the scope, about half have trouble writing them properly, and two-thirds work with no guideline at all. Other researchers note that teams rarely publish their questions alongside the finished model, which means the requirements are often lost.

I find that reassuring, not discouraging. Thirty years of practice has produced a clear record of where the method breaks: vague questions, questions nobody can check, question sets that drift away from the scenarios that justified them, and requirements that live in one person’s head. Those are the failures a prompt list has today, and the knowledge engineering literature has names and partial remedies for each of them. One recent classification separates scoping questions, which mark out what a model should cover, from validating questions, which check whether what it says is correct. That split maps directly onto the two things a brand wants to know: whether it appears in the answer at all, and whether what the answer says about it is true.

The method does not transfer whole, and the reason matters. A knowledge model is deterministic: you run the formal query, and it returns the answer, or it does not. A language model is probabilistic, so the same question produces different answers across runs, phrasings, and engines, and the result is a rate instead of a pass or fail. You also do not own the thing being tested. A knowledge engineer who finds a failed question fixes the model, while you can only change the material the model draws on.

My adaptation, which is my own extension and not something the literature prescribes, is to run each competency question as two tests in a fixed order. First test your own content, which is deterministic: can a person find the expected answer, stated plainly, on a page you control or in a source you can influence? That is a pass or a fail, and you can fix a fail yourself. Only then test the language model by asking the question in several phrasings, several times, across the engines your buyers use, and recording how often the expected answer comes back. A critical survey of GEO research recommends three to five phrasings per information need, which is a sensible floor.

The order matters because a language model that fails a question your own content cannot answer has told you nothing about the language model. In an earlier piece, I argued that AI visibility is three separate problems on three layers, and this is the diagnostic step that tells you which layer to look at. It also clarifies the relationship between a question and a prompt. The competency question is the requirement and the prompts are test cases for it, so twenty phrasings of one question are still one requirement, and a list of three hundred prompts may cover far fewer needs than it appears to.

To make this concrete, take DuaneRoll, a payroll software company I invented for this article. It sells to businesses with 50 to 500 employees, and its motivating scenario is a finance leader whose company has just hired in a third state and who asks an AI assistant what to do about payroll. Here are five competency questions for it.

The fifth question is the one most prompt lists lack. An AI answer that credits you with a service you do not offer creates a support problem at best, and as I wrote about the German court rulings, an answer built from accurate facts attached to the wrong company can become a legal one. Testing for what should not be said is as much a requirement as testing for what should.

Notice what the bad question has in common with most tracked prompts. It sounds like something a buyer would ask, it produces an answer every time, and the answer can be scored for sentiment. It fails as a requirement because there is nothing to check it against.

Every expected answer above has a named owner, and that is deliberate. In knowledge engineering, a domain expert stands behind each expected answer. A prompt test usually has no such person, and the result gets pasted into a report with no record of which model, which version, which date, or whether web search was on. Sascha Donner, writing this year in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, argues that text from a language model lacks the testimonial grounding documents have always had, and that it becomes a usable document only when a person fixes it in a form and takes responsibility for it. The same applies to a test result. An expected answer needs a witness, meaning a named person who will say it is correct, and a logged result needs its conditions recorded, or it is an anecdote with a percentage attached.

Once the questions exist, most of the measurement decisions make themselves. Each question says what to look for, each expected answer says what counts as correct, each owner says who to ask when the answer changes, and each scenario says why the question deserves a place in the set. Sampling, which the industry has learned to do well, then operates on a set that means something. A score built that way can be explained to a chief marketing officer in one sentence: Of the things buyers need to know about us, this is the share the engines get right.

One caution before you hand the job to a machine. Asking an AI system to write your competency questions and grade the answers is tempting, and researchers are actively studying it. A study using 1,393 competency questions found that human evaluators’ performance dropped when the AI assistant gave them incorrect guidance. A language model can draft candidate questions quickly, and a person who knows the business still has to decide which ones are requirements.

A competency question set for a brand is a short, owned list of what buyers must be able to learn about you, each item traceable to a real buying situation and paired with an answer someone will vouch for. Start with 10. Write the scenario, the question, the expected answer, and the owner; check your own content first, and only then look at what the engines say. The method is thirty years old, its weaknesses are well documented, and it is still more than most prompt lists have behind them.

Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”?

RELATED ARTICLEProPublica wanted to find more sources in the federal government. So it brought a truck.Neel DhaneshaMarch 31, 2025ProPublica reported on potential plans to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.”

But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece:

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer.

Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint.

Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip.

“That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.”

We’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting.

ProPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera said. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line.

During a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by.

“We’re always looking for ways to reach the people we need to reach, in the places they’re likeliest to be, based on our reporting needs,” Mel Kramer, engagement team product manager, said. “A good tips line is both staffed and comes to mind quickly. Ryann Hogan and Jay Schwedelson showed how to turn customer questions into useful pages, test content changes for AI search, and keep editors in control.

If customers keep asking whether you offer a service, you have a brief for a landing page. You also have the words people use to describe what they need. That gives an editor a better starting point than asking AI to come up with a topic from scratch.

In 9 AI Workflows That Turn Marketing Data Into Content AI Cites, Ryann Hogan, director of growth marketing at CallRail, and Jay Schwedelson, founder and CEO of Guru Media Hub, tackled two sides of the same problem: how to find something worth publishing and how to tell whether the right people found it.

Hogan used customer conversations to explain what a traffic report can miss. A campaign might generate plenty of calls, but how many ended in a booked appointment? A caller might also say a neighbor recommended the business. The campaign that brought someone to the phone and the reason they knew to look for the company are both useful, but they answer different questions.

Hogan suggested looking for recurring service questions in call summaries. If people keep asking whether a business does a particular kind of work, a page that answers that question in their own terms gives them a reason to visit. If a keyword generates inquiries from people who need something else entirely, the better decision may be to move the budget rather than write more copy.

She applied the same principle to outreach. Before writing a personalized opener, her team checked whether the prospect was in a market it served and offered the services its software supported. She recommended trying the criteria on ten accounts and inspecting the results before running them across a list.

Hogan distinguished between a saved set of instructions and a connector. The first tells the AI how the team writes: examples of its voice, phrases to avoid, the structure of a page and the fields an editor expects. The second lets it do something with that work, such as placing the copy in the right fields in WordPress.

An attendee asked whether that meant giving AI permission to publish. Hogan said her team used draft access and recommended checking with IT and security before connecting a CMS. The editor checked that the copy landed in the right fields, but the review went beyond proofreading. A relevant video, for example, could answer a reader’s question better than another paragraph.

Schwedelson said lists, how-to guides and original research stood out in his team’s review of content cited by AI tools. For a page already on the site, he showed how he asked an AI tool to identify the passages it could use to answer a question and the ones that added little. The result was an editing suggestion, not proof that the page had been cited.

He also suggested testing a change on some pages before rolling it out everywhere. For a set of evergreen articles, he proposed adding a date to the headlines of genuinely updated pieces, leaving a comparison group alone, then comparing traffic over 30 days. In the Q&A he clarified that the date should reflect the current period, not a future one. A difference in traffic would give an editor something to investigate. It would not establish that a date earned an AI citation.

When an attendee asked what a good citation rate looked like, Hogan declined to name a universal target. She suggested comparing performance with the previous month. Schwedelson added a useful check: look at why a business was cited. More mentions for a service it does not offer are hardly a win. Hogan’s preferred measure, where attribution was possible, was whether the marketing produced revenue.

Hogan described a recurring report that refreshed the figures in Google Sheets before she opened it. She used that data to update monthly slides, but kept the judgment about what had changed and what to tell her boss. Hogan explained the distinction: “We still own the numbers. AI is doing the pulling, the formatting, the hard stuff, and then we’re doing the analysis.” See the full on-demand clip at 20:08.

To try that division of labor on your next report:

#7320. Newsletters, obits, and the world’s longest yard sale: How some local news sites saw their traffic spike

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

It’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

Today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in New York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

W42ST In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire. In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

“A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”

O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said.

Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski.

The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

“We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”

Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said.

In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said.

In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”

The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

#7319. Senior Performance Marketing Manager at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

#7317. Why Podcasts Are The B2B Growth Channel Search Can’t Replace

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

As AI answers absorb search clicks, B2B podcasts build trust and earn AI citations. See what works, what fails, and what to measure.

When HubSpot’s blog lost about 80% of its organic traffic to AI, revenue still grew nearly 20%.

In his interview with Greg Jarboe for Search Engine Journal, CMO Kipp Bodnar explained why. In short, HubSpot had been building an audience outside search since 2021: a podcast network in 2021, a newsletter acquisition the same year, a creator program in 2022, and a YouTube network in 2023.

As a result, those newer channels now bring in about 90% of HubSpot’s content leads, with the blog accounting for roughly 10%

I’ve spent six years inside one of those channels. The agency I founded has produced more than 300 B2B podcasts since 2019 and booked more than 2,500 guest appearances for the companies behind them. (Disclosure: All first-hand figures in this article come from that work.) Reading the interview, what struck me wasn’t the traffic drop. Instead, it was that HubSpot’s recovery ran on the channel I know best, and that most of the patterns Bodnar described show up in our data every month, including the uncomfortable ones.

So this article is about what a podcast does for a B2B company that a search result can’t. I’ve organized it around the four things a buyer has to do before they buy from you: notice you, hear you, trust you, and name you. It also covers where podcasts fail because a lot of them do!

Bodnar’s most useful admission was that much of HubSpot’s lost traffic “was never going to turn into revenue.” For example, posts on famous quotes and emojis drew millions of visitors who would never buy software. When AI Overviews answered those questions directly, the visits disappeared, and very few of them were potential customers.

The mechanism is now well documented. Pages ranking first lose 58% of their clicks when an AI Overview appears, according to Ahrefs, up from 34.5% in its April 2025 run. Similarly, Pew Research found users click a standard result 8% of the time when a summary appears, against 15% without.

However, the important point is not that clicks fell. It is that search was always a weak way to build the thing B2B buyers actually use to decide: trust in a specific company, earned from people they already believe.

Reddit and SurveyMonkey’s 2026 research found 73% of B2B decision-makers trust peer recommendations, more than vendor websites at 55%. Meanwhile, Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience. In other words, buyers want to learn from people like them, without being sold to. A 40-minute conversation between two practitioners is exactly that, in a form Google never ranked well, and AI engines are citing more and more.

See also: The Dangerous Seduction Of Click-Chasing

First, a podcast has to get a buyer to notice the company behind it. This is where most B2B shows fail, and I’ve watched this many times.

A company launches a show. The CEO hosts. Twelve episodes later, downloads are flat at 150 per episode, the CEO is bored, and the show quietly stops. The conclusion drawn is “podcasts don’t work for us.” In reality, the problem is that the show launched into nothing.

Across the shows we’ve produced, the ones that grow are the ones that start with an audience to grow from. Specifically, two things happen before episode one. The host appears as a guest on other shows the target buyers already listen to, so the first listeners arrive from a voice they trust. And the guest list is built from people with their own audiences, who then share the episode they’re in.

HubSpot did a version of this at scale. The creator program and the podcast network were built years before the search traffic fell, so there was an audience waiting. Bodnar’s line that “no AEO trick would have covered an 80% hole” is therefore the same lesson at a different size.

See also: The New Organic Growth Stack: Search, Social, Communities & AI

The second job is getting the buyer to listen.

Instantly’s 2026 benchmark puts the average cold email reply rate at 3.43% across its platform, with the top 10% of senders getting past 10%. Instantly sells outbound software, so it has no reason to make those numbers look worse than they are.

A podcast appearance inverts the dynamic. The buyer pressed play and they chose to spend 20 or 40 minutes with your leader, often while doing something else. A host they already trust vouched for your leader in the first 30 seconds.

When we track what happens after client appearances, the pattern is consistent. Inquiries arrive weeks later and quote the episode. In other words, the buyer heard the whole argument before they ever spoke to sales.

For example, we regularly see leads come inbound to our clients saying: “I loved the episode on X with Y, I’d love to chat about Y for our business.”

The same applies to a company’s own show once it has listeners. Edison Research’s Infinite Dial 2026 puts monthly podcast listening at 58% of Americans aged 12 and over. The audience exists, but the question is whether your show gives them a reason to be in it, which brings us to the guests.

The most reliable finding across our shows is also the one most companies resist. The fastest way into a buyer’s world is to interview them. Not a thought leader, not a partner, not a customer success story. The person you want to sell to.

One client, a risk-management software company, launched a weekly show in September 2025 hosted by its CEO, with guests drawn from the safety and risk leaders at its target accounts. (Disclosure: The company is a client of my agency, and these figures are from its public case study.) Twelve months later, roughly 20% of guests have become paying customers. The company also reported a 3.5x return on closed deals in the first six months, with more in the pipeline. Listeners who were never guests have become customers too, citing specific episodes as the reason they reached out.

What made it work wasn’t production quality. Rather, it was three operational choices: a CEO who turned up every week, a conversation format that sets up a follow-up without being a pitch, and a post-recording workflow that got the sales team involved within days of each interview.

Remove any of the three and the show becomes content. With all three, it is a pipeline channel that happens to publish audio.

This is also the part of podcasting that search can’t replicate, and never could. A buyer who spends an hour as a guest on your show has a relationship with your company. By contrast, a buyer who clicked your blog post has a session.

See also: How To Run A Webinar Program That Actually Drives ROI

The fourth outcome is the one Search Engine Journal readers will care about most, because it is where podcasts and AI search meet.

Bodnar made two points about how HubSpot gets cited in AI answers. First, the engines lean on sources that aren’t your site: Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, and review sites. Second, prompts now run 40 to 100 words, so content has to “answer the full question in plain, chunked language, the way a buyer would ask it.” Consequently, HubSpot moved from “The Ultimate Guide to Content Marketing” to hyper-specific pieces built around real buyer situations.

A podcast produces both of those things as a by-product. Every guest appearance is a mention, a link in show notes, and a transcript on someone else’s domain, which is the third-party presence engines weigh. Likewise, every episode of your own show is a transcript of a real buyer describing a real problem in their own words. That is the specific, first-party material engines can’t find anywhere else.

We tested this on our own site. From June 1, 2026, we published one page a day written from our episode transcripts and case studies. Over the following months, our daily AI citations, which had sat between roughly 40 and 80 a day since the previous November, climbed to between 250 and 350 a day by October, and the number of our pages being cited rose from about 15 to around 60:

Daily AI citations and cited pages for the author’s website, November 2025 to October 2026. Image created by the author.

That said, I’d be cautious about the size of that effect. The base was small, and Bodnar is right that attribution here is correlative. But the direction matched what HubSpot saw: AI-answer visitors converting at roughly three times the rate of traditional search, because the buyer has already had the conversation.

The practical implication for anyone running SEO is a show’s transcripts are a content source your competitors cannot copy, and the guest appearances are citations you don’t have to pitch for. Yet most companies with podcasts are sitting on both and using neither.

The wins above come with a long tail of shows that didn’t make it. Three failures account for most of them.

The show launches before anyone has borrowed an audience or booked the host on other shows. Twelve episodes, then silence. This is the majority of B2B podcast failures.

Downloads are the podcast equivalent of the sessions Bodnar says HubSpot watched for 15 years. They are inflated by bots and repeat fetches, and they say nothing about who listened.

Instead, the numbers that matter are which companies are listening, which guests became opportunities, and whether prospects mention the show when they inquire. If your hosting can’t tell you the first of those, you are flying blind.

The interview ends, the episode publishes, and then the guest never hears from the company again. The 20% conversion rate above came from a workflow, not a microphone.

Greg Jarboe ended his write-up of the interview by arguing that the goal has changed. Inbound marketing was about showing up when a buyer searched. Now the buyer asks an AI first, and your company has to be the one they pick afterward. I agree, and I’d add that search alone can’t solve that problem.

Buyers choose companies they have noticed, heard, trusted, and seen named. The places those four things happen are feeds, shows, and AI answers, not result pages.

A podcast is the one channel that can do all four at once. It borrows an audience through guesting, earns listening time no outbound sequence can, builds relationships with the buyers you interview, and produces the specific, first-party content AI engines cite. However, it is also slow, operationally demanding, and easy to do badly, which is why most of them stop at episode 12.

HubSpot built these channels with a large marketing team and a head start of several years. Most B2B companies have neither. That is an argument for starting now, not for not starting.

So before you count downloads, count buyers. How many of the people you want to sell to have been on your show, or listened to it?

Tom Hunt is the founder and CEO of Fame, a leading B2B podcasting company. With over seven years of experience ...

#7315. Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in New Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

In other words, the generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

Then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger users, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

My data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It shows up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

Third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest users are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and says they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University and a faculty associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University.

#7312. Paid Search Has An AI Blind Spot – IAB Blueprint Says A Claim Is Not Credit via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Paid search may be booking sales that AI assistants created. The IAB’s new blueprint sets a standard of evidence, with four steps to test it in Google Ads.

If your branded search campaigns have posted their best return on ad spend of the year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) has a question you should answer before you ask for more budget. Who, or what, created that demand in the first place?

On Nov. 12, the IAB released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework for sorting out what role AI played when someone buys something. The report cites Similarweb data showing that consumers who got a brand recommendation from an AI assistant were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within seven days. Only 8.8% of those visits came directly from AI referrals. Search was credited with 55.9% of them, and direct traffic with 19.9%.

ChatGPT answer can create the intent, a branded query can capture it, and your Google Ads account can book the conversion as a brand campaign win.

The blueprint won’t tell you how much of your brand revenue fits that description. What it does give you is a standard of evidence for finding out, plus a few habits worth adopting in your accounts before the 2027 planning cycle locks in.

The framework asks three questions of each conversion. Who or what created the intent? Who or what made the decision? Who or what completed the purchase?

The answers put the conversion in one of three pathways, labeled Human-Owned, AI-Assisted, and AI-Executed. According to AdExchanger’s account of the document:

The pathway then decides which parties are eligible to make a “decision claim” or a “contributory claim,” and what evidence each claim needs. The IAB’s release says, “A claim is not credit; it is the right to be evaluated for credit.”

Caroline Giegerich, the IAB’s VP of AI, framed the problem in terms every search marketer will recognize.

“AI-influenced sales are sometimes reported as search or direct traffic, which can send the next marketing investment to the wrong channel,” she said in the announcement. She added that the blueprint is meant to work alongside existing attribution systems, defining the extra credit claims AI creates and the evidence each one requires.

In other words, nobody is asking you to rip out data-driven attribution. The blueprint sits on top of it.

The document also changed shape while it was being written. Giegerich told Digiday she went in expecting the working group to work out how credit gets assigned, and the document became “more of a call to action to the industry” instead. Digiday reported the effort took about four months and named working group members including People Inc., Walmart, WPP Media, Emberos, Criteo, Bluefish, Microsoft, Brandlight, Tinuiti, and Prudential Financial.

Google is not among the members Digiday named, which matters for anyone hoping the largest search ad platform will start labeling AI-originated activity the way the blueprint asks.

See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore

The IAB grounded the release in its own buyer research. In the 2026 Outlook Study: September Update, 45% of ad buyers named comparing AI-driven and traditional customer journeys as their top measurement challenge, and 44% said they rely on branded search and direct traffic as proxies for AI influence they can’t track.

Google’s own numbers show why this is getting harder to ignore. Alphabet reported Q3 2026 Google Search & other revenue of $63.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year, while CEO Sundar Pichai said Search query growth was the fastest it has been in five years. On the earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler pointed to lower monetization of fast-growing AI Mode queries as one factor in the slower revenue growth, alongside currency effects, which he called the largest factor. More queries are flowing through AI surfaces, and the trail from those surfaces to the conversion is thinner than the trail from a classic results page.

Here is my perspective. The most useful line in the blueprint for PPC managers, is that a claim is not credit. Platform attribution has blurred those two ideas for as long as I’ve covered this business, since 2003. Google Ads data-driven attribution spreads credit across the Google touchpoints it can observe. It cannot observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent someone to type your brand name. So, the report you trust most has a blind spot exactly where the new demand is being created.

See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It

Before anyone builds a budget case on 55.9%, it helps to know where that figure comes from.

It originates in Similarweb’s June 2026 study, “The Downstream Impact of AI Visibility.” It used Similarweb’s U.S. desktop panel from July through December 2025, looked at ChatGPT recommendations, and studied three verticals through brand pairs (American Express and Capital One, Skyscanner and Kayak, Sephora and Ulta). Users who named the brand in their own prompt were excluded.

Search accounted for 55.9% of AI-influenced visits versus 40.4% of visits that weren’t AI-influenced, a gap of 15.5 points. Direct traffic went the other way, 19.9% versus 38.8%. AI-influenced visitors also viewed about 12 pages per visit, compared with 6.5 for everyone else.

There are limits a practitioner should keep in view. The panel is desktop only, while a large share of shopping happens on phones. It covers ChatGPT, not Claude, Copilot, Gemini, or Google’s own AI Mode. Six brands is a small sample, and the published figures I could find report “search” as a channel without splitting paid clicks from organic ones, so nobody should claim from this study that a specific share went to Google Ads.

One more caution about the IAB survey. MediaPost reported that 44% of buyers named adapting to changing consumer behavior, including AI-driven search, as their top investment challenge. The release for the blueprint cites 44% relying on branded search and direct traffic as proxies. Same study, same percentage, different questions.

Google Analytics added an “AI Assistant” channel to GA4’s Default Channel Group in May 2026, which sorts sessions from recognized chatbot referrers into their own row. It’s a real improvement, but it works on referrers. The shopper who reads a ChatGPT answer, opens a new tab, and searches your brand shows up as Paid Search or Organic Search, never as AI Assistant. That is the exact behavior the Similarweb data describes.

See also: 81.8% Of My ‘AI Assistant’ Traffic Was Fake. The Googlebot Number Was Worse

In the first edition of YouTube and Video Marketing, published in 2009, I quoted Galileo on page 337. “Count what is countable, measure what is measurable. What is not measurable, make measurable.” I’ve repeated it to students and clients ever since, because I haven’t found a better summary of what a marketer’s job is.

The IAB blueprint reads like a working version of it for paid search.

Count what is countable. Clicks, conversions, and sessions with an AI referrer are all countable, and your accounts already count them well.

Measure what is measurable. Whether your brand campaigns create sales or simply catch them on the way to checkout can be measured with lift tests and holdouts. Most advertisers just haven’t done it.

Then comes the hard part: What is not measurable, make measurable. Nobody outside the AI platforms can observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent a shopper to type your brand name into Google. The blueprint’s answer is to classify that conversion anyway, attach a claim to it, and spell out the evidence the claim would need. That is how something unmeasurable starts becoming measurable. It also tells you exactly what to ask for when the AI platforms are ready to share.

None of this requires the AI platforms to cooperate first. Here are four steps you can take now.

1. Estimate your pathway mix. The blueprint’s first ask of brands is to estimate the share of their conversions in each pathway. The cheapest way to start is to ask customers. Add AI assistant options (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Copilot, Claude) to your post-purchase survey or lead form’s “how did you hear about us” question. Store the answer in your CRM. If you already import offline conversions, you can bring a self-reported “AI-assisted” signal into Google Ads as a separate conversion action set to secondary, so you can see it by campaign without letting it steer Smart Bidding.

2. Put brand campaigns through an incrementality test. Google Ads help documentation now lists Search and Performance Max as supported campaign types for user-based Conversion Lift, with thresholds of at least 1,000 observed conversions and a minimum study campaign budget of $5,000. The same page still notes that Conversion Lift isn’t available for every account, so check with your rep. If you don’t qualify, a geo-based holdout on brand terms will tell you something useful. A lift test won’t classify the AI pathway for you. It will tell you how much of what your brand campaign claims would have happened anyway, which is the question you need answered before brand spend absorbs more of the budget.

3. Report two columns, not one. The blueprint asks agencies to apply a single claim-and-evidence standard across platforms and to separate platform-reported claims from independently verified ones. Do that in your next Quarterly Business Review (QBR). Show Google Ads-reported brand conversions next to lift-tested incremental conversions, and show GA4’s AI Assistant sessions next to your survey’s self-reported AI share. When the columns disagree, that disagreement is the finding.

4. Ask your platform reps how AI traffic is labeled. The blueprint asks AI platforms to disclose whether recommendations are paid or organic, to name the sources behind them, and to label AI-originated traffic consistently. Put those questions to your Google and Microsoft Advertising reps directly, especially about how clicks and conversions from ads in AI Mode and Copilot surface in your reports. Microsoft sat on the working group. Its answers may come faster.

The IAB is candid that this is a framework, not a fix. CEO David Cohen said the blueprint “is honest about what the industry can’t yet substantiate.” Much of the evidence needed to support AI claims either isn’t captured or sits inside the AI platforms.

I’d go further. The PPC managers who wait for ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI Mode to hand over clean, labeled data will spend 2027 defending brand budgets with numbers they can’t explain to a CFO. The ones who start estimating their pathway mix now, with surveys, lift tests, and two-column reporting, will at least be counting the right things.
