#7311. The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Many publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

As part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

“As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” said Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”

The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent company, News Corp.

“We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”

Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the company’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

“One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”

More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

Many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

Known Agents currently tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

“Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” said King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”

King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

“It’s been such a manual process,” said King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”

Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the company’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

“We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, said. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”

Lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he said.

Slate currently has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

“It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” said Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”

#7308. Google Says Promotion Mode Now Supports Shopping Campaigns via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Standard Shopping campaigns can use Promotion Mode to lower Target ROAS for short sales, with an optional extra daily budget, an updated help page says.

Retailers using standard Shopping campaigns can now schedule a lower Target ROAS and, if they choose, add extra daily budget for a 3- to 14-day sale with Promotion Mode, according to Google’s updated help page.

The page says Promotion Mode is supported for “standard Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns” and is in an open beta.

Shopping wasn’t part of the beta at launch. Google’s June 15 announcement said, “This beta is available for Search and Performance Max campaigns.” SEJ’s Brooke Osmundson reported the beta that day.

As of Nov. 27, the page in several other languages, including German, French and Spanish, still lists only Search and Performance Max, and the English page doesn’t say when Shopping support was added.

The Target ROAS for a campaign will be lowered by a tolerance of 5% to 90% in Promotion Mode. In the page’s example, a Target ROAS of 500% with a 20% tolerance would equal a new Target ROAS of 400%.

You may add an extra amount to spend each day above your baseline on an average daily budget; however, this isn’t available on a campaign total budget. To increase spending on a campaign total budget during a promotion, you’ll need to raise the total manually.

Google’s June launch example shows where advertisers set promotion dates, Target ROAS tolerance, and the optional extra daily budget.

Target ROAS bidding must be enabled at the campaign level. Portfolio bid strategies and shared budgets are not currently supported. Campaigns which have run experiments previously are also unable to use Promotion Mode.

Regardless of whether Exploration has been toggled on for a campaign, Smart Bidding Exploration will automatically be on while it’s running in Promotion Mode. When Exploration is enabled before a campaign enters Promotion Mode, the two settings’ tolerances will be combined. In Google’s example, 20% plus 20% makes 40%.

In Performance Max campaigns running Promotion Mode, Google’s help documentation explains that Smart Bidding Exploration “applies to both Search and Shopping inventory” as well as text and Shopping ads. However, if a campaign is largely serving on other networks, you may see less impact from this Smart Bidding feature. The page’s translations into various languages still say that the exploration begins with only Search inventory.

The English version also details where an active promotion is shown (campaign settings, campaign tables, the Seasonality Adjustment menu and the bid strategy and budget reports) and says these changes are being rolled out incrementally and may not be available in all accounts at this time.

Retailers that lower Shopping targets and raise daily budgets manually during a sale can schedule these changes in advance and have them revert once the sale has concluded.

As for timing, Google’s page says new campaigns should be created at least 48 hours in advance of a promotion’s start date, and existing campaigns should operate for at least one complete conversion cycle on a daily budget before turning on Promotion Mode. After an active promotion begins, its start date cannot be modified, and changes to the Target ROAS and average daily budget will need to be done through the Promotion Mode settings. Further, Google recommends avoiding CPC bid caps and suggests allowing 1-2 conversion cycles once a promotion ends for Smart Bidding to adjust to large target or budget changes.

When measuring results from a Promotion Mode sale, Google says to account for the lowered target in the bid strategy report. A promotion can be ended early, and once it’s running, its end date can move as long as the whole promotion stays within 14 days.

#7301. Google Moves 404 Guidance To Search Central, Adds A 410 Crawl Note via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google moved its 404 guidance into Search Central and now says 410s generally get crawled less often, while treating both codes the same for indexing.

Returning a 410 status code for a removed page “generally leads to less frequent crawling,” according to Google’s updated guide to crawling errors. For indexing, Google treats 404 and 410 the same.

The line arrived on Nov. 27 in a new section on deciding whether to fix 404 errors reported in Search Console. The documentation changelog says the section brings 404 guidance over from the Search Console Help Center into Search Central documentation, and the old Help page now redirects to the guide.

Most of the section revisits advice Google had already shared, but its 410 line offers a different take from the Help page. The retired page read, “Currently Google treats 410s (Gone) the same as 404s (Not found).”

Google’s new guidelines have separated crawling of pages with 404 or 410 status codes from how they are indexed by Google. For a URL that was crawled by Google but returned a 404 status code, Google’s crawlers “might continue checking it occasionally,” the guide says. The frequency of crawling is generally reduced once Google receives a 410 status code, and a 410 is treated like a 404 when it comes to indexing.

When I covered John Mueller’s comments on the two codes in April 2024, he called the difference in processing “so minimal” that he couldn’t think of a time he’d prefer one over the other for SEO purposes. The new guide keeps the codes equal for indexing and names a difference in crawling.

Google’s guide puts the crawl-frequency distinction in its advice on removing URLs from sitemaps.

The rest of the new section repeats points from the old Help page and from a Google video embedded in the guide. One of them is a warning against blocking 404 URLs in robots.txt, since Google has to crawl a URL to see its status code. Roger Montti covered the video on Oct. 29.

For removed pages, the crawling errors guide says to take the URLs out of sitemaps. For live pages that shouldn’t appear in Search, Google’s sitemaps overview now says leaving a URL out of a sitemap “doesn’t prevent Google from crawling or indexing it” when other pages link to it. The overview points to noindex for those pages instead.

Sites bulk removing pages, such as an archive of discontinued products, can use a documented crawl difference when deciding which pages should receive a 404 vs. a 410 for content that is permanently deleted. According to Google’s crawling error guidelines, regardless of which of these codes you use, the code will not limit a site’s crawl capacity, and previously crawled 404 URLs “don’t meaningfully consume crawl budget.”

Whichever you decide on, delete your old URLs from your sitemaps and do not block them in robots.txt.

Google’s guide doesn’t specify how much less often URLs that return a 410 are crawled. A site that retires many pages can explore the impact in its server logs by returning a 410 for one group of similar removed URLs and a 404 for another.

#7292. Core Updates, Ranking Feedback, Google-Agent & WordPress – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

One core update is done and the next is announced, plus how to send update feedback, let a user-triggered agent past bot rules, and answer a goodbye SEO post.

Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates cover how to measure and respond to core updates, whether Google’s agent gets past your defenses, and what you can, and can’t, assume about a site’s CMS.

Google finished its November core update and announced December’s, published pages on update notice and feedback, and explained how to let Google-Agent through bot defenses. WordPress’s share of the web fell nearly 5 points in a year in W3Techs’ survey, and Salesforce’s CEO said goodbye to SEO while a Salesforce guide calls SEO the foundation.

Here’s what matters for you and your work.

Google’s November 2026 core update finished rolling out on Nov. 24. About an hour later, Google preannounced a December core update on the Search Status Dashboard.

Key facts: The November update began on Nov. 10, wrapping up within the two-week window Google set at launch. Google’s December entry explains that the update focuses on how its systems “understand and rank relevant content (including for longer and more complex questions)” and on “improving personalized results for people who have personalization turned on.” It’s “scheduled to be released in December 2026,” with no date given.

Google advises waiting for no less than a complete week of data after an update is finished, then comparing that week to a week prior to the rollout date. For this update, the first week would be from Nov. 25 through Dec. 1, which includes U.S. Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, while December’s update may start as early as Dec. 1. Use Search Console to create a custom annotation for Nov. 24, and one for December’s start date as soon as that date has been posted.

In the Add Annotation dialog, choose a date and enter a short note.

Read our full coverage: Google Confirms November 2026 Core Update Is Complete and Google Announces December 2026 Core Update Ahead Of Rollout

Google’s newest pages in the ranking section of Search Central provide guidance for when Google gives notice of ranking and policy changes, how to submit feedback regarding those changes, and the UK appeals process which will begin Dec. 17.

Key facts: Google’s stay-informed page states that the company gives notice of actionable policy changes and significant ranking changes like core updates. Notice of potential ranking changes that may significantly affect UK users is provided to site owners and follows the fair ranking requirements established by the United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). Verified site owners may provide feedback using Search Console’s Submit Feedback button, including identifying the specific change via a hashtag, such as #NovemberCoreUpdate2026. However, according to Google, this type of feedback does not trigger manual ranking adjustments for individual URLs. Beginning Dec. 17, sites that provide service to UK users and have been manually removed from Google’s index as a whole can pursue an appeal through the UK CMA indexing appeal process.

The stay-informed page states you need to wait until an update is marked complete and then for at least one more week, prior to assessing if there have been any traffic changes, and it lists feedback as a next step. For the November update, a submission that includes a Performance report snapshot (once the data has rolled into Search Console), the specific queries and URLs affected by the update, and the associated hashtag can include data from the week through Dec. 1. Google lists pre-announcements, roll-out dates and completion notifications on its dashboard, so subscribing to its RSS feed will tell you when the next pre-announcement is posted.

Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Send Feedback On A Core Update

On Nov. 17, Google added a guide to its crawling documentation on letting Google-Agent through CDNs, web application firewalls (WAFs) and bot-detection services. Google-Agent is the name its agents use to navigate sites and take actions for users.

Key facts: Google-Agent requests have “Google-Agent” within the User-Agent header and are coming from an IP address listed in Google’s user-triggered-agents.json file and requests in Google’s Web Bot Auth experiment are carrying a digital signature. Verified requests should bypass bot challenges according to the guide. Troubleshooting includes checking the priority of rules, CAPTCHAs on search and form submissions, actions (add-to-cart, booking), and rate limits on shared IP addresses. The guide does not mention what products within Google utilize Google-Agent.

For sites that want to welcome Google-Agent, the key is to make sure the verified rule sits above managed bot rules and AI agent category blocks. It should also cover on-site search, cart, booking and API requests, not just the first page an agent loads.

Read our full coverage: Google Publishes Guidance For Google-Agent Crawler

As of Nov. 23, WordPress powered 38.4% of all websites in W3Techs’ daily-updated survey, down from 43.2% a year earlier.

Key facts: Over the same year, the share of sites running none of the CMSs W3Techs tracks rose 4.4 points, from 28.6% to 33.0%. That group can include sites with no CMS and sites on a CMS W3Techs doesn’t track.

On a third of the sites surveyed by W3Techs, it’s not safe to assume a WordPress SEO plugin or another platform’s defaults are handling titles, canonicals, robots meta, or sitemaps. An audit or pitch has to start by finding out what’s in place, if anything.

Read our full coverage: WordPress Drops To 38.4% Of The Web, Down Nearly 5 Points In A Year

On Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff ended his post on X advertising Palmata, an AI product from Salesforce that tracks what AI assistants say about a company, with the statement “Goodbye SEO. Hello Palmata!” Salesforce also has a guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) that addresses how new business owners can do well at both, and it states “SEO is still the foundation.”

Key facts: According to Benioff’s post, customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead ask their AI assistants which brands they should purchase from. The guide, written by Graham Hardt, who is identified as a senior director of SEO, was published Sept. 11 and states SEO “isn’t going away,” but also that relying on SEO alone “creates a blind spot” for new businesses.

When Benioff’s post reaches a marketing executive, Salesforce’s September guide offers a case for both SEO and AEO, describing them as “two visibility layers for the same audience.” It also recommends, “Track both sets of metrics,” including organic traffic and rankings alongside AI citation monitoring.

Read our full coverage: Salesforce CEO Says ‘Goodbye SEO.’ Salesforce’s SEO Guide Disagrees

Every story this week evaluates an assumption that SEO teams have usually taken as given. November’s core update provided a post-update week that takes in Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with another core update set for next month. For its significant ranking and policy updates, Google’s new pages put formal notice, along with a mechanism to provide feedback, in writing. A website’s bot defense systems can block the actions of Google’s own agent. According to results of a recent survey, about a third of the web properties it covers operate without any of the CMSs tracked by W3Techs. Two months prior to the Salesforce CEO’s statement, “Goodbye SEO,” a Salesforce guide called SEO the foundation. This week’s task is to determine whether those long-held assumptions still apply to your individual websites.

#7289. Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at Clutch

Clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

As a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

This is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

You build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

This role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice

You'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

The operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end

Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live

Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff

Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip

Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production

Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work

Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM

Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild

Have taken one net-new agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner

Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change

Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you

Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field

7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). #7287. Pinterest announces partnership with Microsoft Ads

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The integration will see Pinterest ad placements extended across Microsoft’s partner platforms.

Pinterest has announced a new integration with Microsoft Advertising, which will make Pinterest ad placements available to Microsoft platform users.

Microsoft Ads is primarily focused on placements within Microsoft’s own ecosystem, but it also incorporates a range of partner sites and platforms, enabling advertisers to expand their promotions. And now, Pinterest will be added to that list of partner platforms.

As explained by Pinterest: “Microsoft Advertising customers’ campaigns will have access to Pinterest’s visual search environment through a custom contextual bidding model. Eligible Microsoft Advertising campaigns can access Pinterest's open-auction inventory across home feed, search, and related Pins, expanding opportunities to engage consumers throughout their discovery journeys.”

Pinterest added that targeting for its Microsoft Ads integration will be built on Pinterest search queries, contextual signals, and first-party intent data.

“[T]he model identifies relevant ad placements across Pinterest’s visual search adjacent inventory,” Pinterest said. “The integration uses Pinterest Intelligence, Pinterest’s AI-powered understanding of people’s interests, combining hundreds of billions of connections with visual-understanding technology and behavioral signals to surface personalized interests and anticipate what users may want next.”

Pinterest has been working to expand its ad business in order to boost its revenue potential. Pinterest's ad intake has been growing, but its third quarter revenue intake fell short of Wall Street expectations, while it's also encountered regulatory restrictions in the EU market.

Last month, Pinterest announced a new partnership with Magnite that will make Pinterest’s ad inventory available via multiple ad exchanges, including Yahoo DSP and Amazon Ads DVA+, as well as Google Display and Video 360.

The new partnership with Microsoft will feed even more ads into Pinterest’s system.

Pinterest said its ad inventory will initially be available via Microsoft Ads in North America, Australia and New Zealand.

#7286. Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

This role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical plans, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

You understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:

Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

Are a fast learner, frequently picking up new languages and tools.

Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

Own the architecture of the GTM systems stack: define how Salesforce, HubSpot, enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and the data platform fit together, and write the technical strategy that guides how it evolves.

Lead build-vs-buy and procurement decisions: evaluate vendors, run proofs of concept, assess security and integration fit, and partner with Director of GTM Systems and Analytics, Finance, Legal, and IT on selection and renewals.

Shape the GTM systems roadmap with senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, RevOps, Finance, and Engineering: align on requirements, sequence investments, make clear tradeoffs, and lead cross-functional initiatives to completion.

Own Salesforce as the engineering system of record for revenue: data model, flows and automation, validation rules, field governance, and access control.

Own HubSpot for campaigns and lead generation, along with the HubSpot-Salesforce sync — so leads, contacts, and engagement signals reach the revenue pipeline without drift or silent failures.

Build and maintain integrations across the GTM stack, and partner with GTM Analytics Engineering on reliable data flows to the central data platform.

Design and deploy agentic workflows that consume GTM data, surface actionable signals, and automate manual operations — and set the patterns and guardrails others build on.

Clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

This is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. #7282. Campaign Trail: Tiffany tells human holiday story with Hollywood talent

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The luxury brand and agency American Haiku leaned into real emotions with actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

In adland, it has been a decidedly handmade holiday season, with brands including Levi’s and E.l.f. turning to techniques like stop-motion animation to connect with consumers who are growing weary of ads created by artificial intelligence.

For its annual holiday effort, Tiffany & Co. found the best way to resonate with consumers is through human storytelling. The luxury brand’s global campaign, “Love is a Gift,” was created with agency American Haiku and revolves around a two-minute film starring actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

The short, “You & Me,” jumps from the present day to New York City in the 1990s to tell the story of a young girl and her mother, played by Seyfried. The girl watches her mother work as a choreographer and has a handful of holiday experiences before being gifted with a Tiffany ornament that she shares with her own daughter in the present.

“Moving between past and present, the film reflects the enduring place Tiffany & Co. holds in life’s most meaningful moments and the stories we carry forward,” said CMO Andrea Davey in a statement.

The film is soundtracked by a cover of The Wannadies’ “You & Me Song,” a tune best known for its appearance on the 1996 “Romeo + Juliet” soundtrack. The campaign will run across cinema, paid and organic social, digital out-of-home, owned channels and clienteling across global channels.

Along with being on-trend with regard to stories imbued with humanity, Tiffany’s holiday campaign also represents a pivot from the brand’s past holiday creative. The 2025 edition of the “Love is a Gift” campaign turned its iconic blue boxes into portals to love stories around the world. This year, Tiffany brought on American Haiku, which had worked on a previous campaign for the brand in the U.K., but didn’t offer a traditional brief.

“They came to us with an initial idea of a family spending the holidays in their home and [tapping] into the memory aspect,” said Ben Muckensturm, creative director at the shop. “Where we pushed the work was bringing in the importance of the mother-daughter relationship that I think is the core of the story.”

Keying into the mother-daughter story gave the brand and agency a larger insight around the memory of seeing a parent as a person in their own world that is relatable to consumers, whether or not they are wealthy residents of the Upper East Side like the characters in the film. In the film, the true gift is not the ornament but the memory that is associated with it.

“That opened us up to how we explore the past and then bring it back to the present and create a piece that feels essentially real, that anyone could connect with,” Muckensturm said. “Everything was shot in New York. It was definitely an intentional push to try to bring it to the real world and make it more of an emotional piece.”

“You & Me” also delivers nostalgia for a pre-digital ‘90s that has been a reliable way to engage millennial audiences. However, the nostalgia in the film is not the traditional touchstones, like technology and boy bands, used by marketers looking to tap into memories of the decade. Instead, Tiffany looked at its own archives and at the holidays of movies like “Home Alone” and “The Parent Trap” for inspiration.

“When we created the town house, we went back to old archival Tiffany imagery of how things were,” Muckensturm said of creating the main set for the ad. “Especially on Fifth Avenue, most of the references that we brought were from ‘Home Alone 2,’ like what the streets looked like at the time. It's great to be able to tap into things that people are familiar with.”

After creating the world of the ad, the agency populated it with brand ambassador Seyfried, whose character is the mother in the past, rather than the main character in the present-day framing device. The actor, an Academy Award nominee whose performance in one of the year’s biggest films has captivated audiences, brought her gifts to the production.

“She has such a maternal instinct that really played perfectly on set, and you could see really how she was a mother to that girl for the days that we shot,” Muckensturm said.

The choice of Cianfrance, a director best known for dramatic fare like “Blue Valentine” and “The Place Beyond the Pines,” helped the brand and agency get the emotional tone right, without rehearsal and without falling into familiar or even corny holiday tropes.

“There was a trusting relationship between production partners, us and the client to come into it with a really open mind to see what the scene gives us,” Muckensturm said. “We knew where we were going to shoot, and we were trying to get a range of emotion… but we really let him direct them and let this play naturally.”

#7278. Pinterest simplifies parental controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform has updated its parental control dashboard to offer a more streamlined way to manage devices and access options.

Pinterest has updated its parental control elements to offer a more integrated, streamlined process and make it easier for parents to manage their child’s in-app experience.

As shown in these example screens, Pinterest’s updated parental controls dashboard now includes all of the app’s oversight and management options in one place, including profile visibility, content recommendations and connection controls.

The updated parental controls also include direct links to manage device-level screen time and location settings. Parents will also be able to make their kids’ profiles private by default and set limits on ad personalization and social features.

In addition, Pinterest added tools that allow parents to control the amount of artificial intelligence-generated content that teens see in the app. There’s also new notification management functionality.

Parents can also decide whether their teens have autoplay video switched on or not, which could help to combat compulsive viewing behaviors.

Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the platform is focused on building an experience that’s age-appropriate for teens from the start, with protections that are built in, “not bolted on.”

“For parents who want more involvement, the controls are easy to find and simple to use,” Ready said. “Families can choose the experience that is right for them, while teens can continue to explore their interests and feel inspired.”

Pinterest has been working to present its app as an alternative to potentially harmful, engagement-focused approaches that have been adopted by other social media platforms.

In September, Pinterest published a report on how teens use the app, which showed that more than 77% of its teen audience uses Pinterest to explore creative interests.

More teen control options will provide additional peace of mind for parents, which could help to further establish Pinterest as a safer space for young users.

#7270. How Jell-O’s new creative platform looks to shift consumer perceptions

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The campaign, the first by Johannes Leonardo for the Kraft Heinz brand, represents its largest marketing investment in more than a decade.

Jell-O on Monday launched a new creative platform, “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” that seeks to shift consumer perceptions about how the product can be enjoyed beyond traditional use cases. The effort represents the Kraft Heinz brand’s largest marketing investment in more than a decade, per details shared with Marketing Dive.

“As a nearly 130-year-old brand, we recognized a disconnect between how familiar consumers are with Jell-O and how often they think to purchase it,” Kathryn O’Brien, head of marketing for desserts at Kraft Heinz, said in emailed comments. “We want Jell-O to be more than something that comes to mind for a bowl of gelatin or pudding, but rather a part of the creative process in the kitchen.”

Central to the campaign are two 15-second spots that show home cooks in monochrome kitchens preparing desserts with Jell-O before a social-inspired flip transition pivots the scene to others marveling over the finished product.

The campaign was created by Johannes Leonardo and is the first campaign for the brand by the agency, which has held creative duties on select Kraft Heinz brands since 2020. The spots were directed by Drew Kirsch, a veteran of music videos who has worked with Taylor Swift, and feature an original electronic-pop song that uses “oh hello, Jell-O” as a vocal hook.

“Rather than borrowing an existing song, we saw an opportunity to build an ownable sonic identity around the platform,” O’Brien said. “The original track is a recognizable brand asset that can extend across social, content and future campaign moments.”

As part of the launch, Jell-O will take over the Las Vegas Sphere this week, transforming the orb into a gelatin mold, a “dirt cup” dessert and banana cream pudding. “Oh Hello, Jell-O” will run across streaming, online video, social and digital throughout 2027, with investment pulsing around key seasonal moments. The significant media investment comes at a pivotal moment for the brand, O’Brien explained.

“Our first-ever CTV buy allows us to bring the campaign's highly visual, music-driven creative to life on the big screen, showcasing the playfulness, vibrant colors and unexpected transformations in a high-attention environment,” the executive said. “We're taking an integrated approach throughout 2027, combining streaming and online video with social, digital and e-commerce touchpoints.”

The creative platform builds on a 2023 rebrand, crafted with agency Brand Opus, that updated Jell-O’s visual identity with a more modern look and feel. The rebrand, which at the time was its first such effort in 10 years, arrived amid an industry-wide move to help CPG brands engage with new consumer groups.

Kraft Heinz in February stopped plans to split its condiment and grocery staples businesses, with CEO Steve Cahillane saying many of the CPG company’s challenges are fixable. The company is pouring $700 million into a turnaround strategy that includes significant investments in marketing, which has been increased to at least 6% of net sales.

While Kraft Heinz saw organic net sales decrease 1.1% in Q3 2026, the company’s market share, sales and volume trends improved in every region, per an earnings report. Jell-O was cited on an earnings call as a brand with which the company is looking to win share by investing selectively.

#7266. Philadelphia whips up bigger holiday marketing spend amid brand revamp

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Brand character Phillyboy returns in a Santa-like role to dish out blocks of cream cheese to be used in cheesecake recipes.

“Really Philly Good,” which debuted in February, was developed to broaden consumer perceptions of what Philadelphia has to offer. Rather than only showing the product as a cold spread for bagels and snacks, the platform highlights how cream cheese can be used to enrich more involved meals. A larger marketing push around Q4 responds to the insight that one-third of Philadelphia cream cheese bricks are sold during the November-December period and Google search trends data that show spikes in interest for cheesecake recipes during the season.

In the new work, Phillyboy acts as a Santa-like figure, trotting into houses saddled on his dairy cow to dole out blocks of cream cheese that are then used to make cheesecake. The rugged Western-themed character is accompanied by a spin on Christmas standards like “Jingle Bells.” Agency Johannes Leonardo is behind “Really Philly Good” while Nalle Sjöblad, from Spark & Riot, directed the holiday ad spots. The full media plan spans TV, streaming, connected TV, online video, social, creators and retail elements.

Beyond video advertising, Philadelphia is running a national integration with “Happy Hour with Ina Garten” that is supported by sponsored social content and a custom cheesecake recipe on the Barefoot Contessa website and Substack. Other social and digital activations include a cheesecake-building experience on Pinterest, an augmented reality Snapchat lens and a focus on TikTok search and trending food and drink Reels content on Meta.

In addition, the Kraft Heinz marketer enlisted TikTok and Instagram creators, including Tineke “Tini” Younger and Kiley O’Donnell, for holiday cheesecake content. The creator program started on Nov. 2 and has so far drawn nearly 1 million organic views and 43,000 engagements, the brand said.

Kraft Heinz is broadly revamping its portfolio as it tries to win back consumers who have shifted toward protein-rich and better-for-you offerings. In August, it announced plans to spend an additional $100 million on its turnaround, with the lion’s share of the investment concentrated in marketing. Marketing will represent at least 6% of the company’s net sales this year.

Jell-O, another brand under Kraft Heinz, unveiled a new creative platform on Monday that is backed by its largest marketing investment in more than a decade. Johannes Leonardo also handled “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” the shop’s first work for the brand.

Carl’s Jr. has appointed David&Goliath as marketing agency of record as it shifts focus to cooked-to-order burgers and tries to revive a bolder, boundary-pushing brand personality, according to news shared with Marketing Dive. Carl’s Jr. did not previously have a dedicated AOR, and instead worked with agencies on a project basis, Marketing Dive understands.

David&Goliath, which is part of Innocean Worldwide, will oversee brand strategy, creative development, experiential marketing, production and storytelling for the fast-food chain, with a mandate to lean into Carl’s Jr.'s heritage while shoring up cultural relevance with younger consumers. Its first work is expected to arrive in Q1 of next year.

CKE Restaurants Holdings-owned Carl’s Jr. unveiled its Burger Revolution strategy in September, which introduces a systemwide cooked-to-order approach to burger preparation. The announcement was accompanied by the release of a limited-time Angus Maximus 5.7-ounce burger. The changes are part of a larger effort by Carl’s Jr. to emphasize food quality, which has manifested in promotional areas like limited-time offerings.

Other fast-food companies, including rival Burger King, have thrown a spotlight on premium ingredients and restaurant improvements to win back price-sensitive diners. Carl’s Jr.’s franchised store count has declined in recent years. Franchisees of the brand and sister restaurant Hardee’s have faced their own profitability struggles, with a major one in Calirfornia in April declaring bankruptcy, Marketing Dive’s sister publication Restaurant Dive previously reported.

Carl’s Jr. has made internal changes to its marketing leadership this year as well. In the spring, CKE Restaurants named Burge Diemer, a restaurant industry vet who previously worked at brands including The Habit Burger & Grill, Boston Market and Jack in the Box, as CMO of Carl’s Jr. Diemer is tasked with developing breakthrough campaigns and driving product innovation. She credited David&Goliath with possessing the bravery necessary to build on Carl’s Jr.’s legacy.

“Together, we’re excited to push boundaries, expand our connection with customers, and bring the unmistakable Carl’s Jr. spirit to a new generation of burger lovers,” Diemer said in a press statement.

Carl’s Jr.’s advertising has not shied away from pushing buttons in the past. The chain in the 2000s became known for TV commercials featuring bikini-clad models suggestively eating burgers. It has dipped back into the racy well in recent years, including through a 2025 campaign with influencer Alix Earle that touted offerings like a hangover-themed burger.

#7260. Meta says social media is key driver for holiday discovery

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

People who shop via social media are more likely to purchase across multiple categories and self-gift, according to the company.

Meta’s has shared some key data notes on shopping activity in its apps, which could provide additional guidance for brands to assist with their holiday campaign planning.

The data was published earlier this year, and is based on research conducted by Ipsos, which surveyed 14,473 shoppers in 18 countries across North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

The data found that social media is a key driver of discovery for holiday season shoppers.

As per Meta: “Across all 18 markets surveyed, 37% of festive shoppers use social media for gift discovery and inspiration. That places it on par with search engines (41%) and ahead of TV advertising (27%).”

The data also showed that video is the most influential content type, while high-quality product photography is also a valuable driver.

The report also looked at what drives purchase decisions among social media shoppers.

While it also explored key spending behaviors.

As per the report: “Social shoppers are far more commercially engaged than the average holiday shopper. They plan to spend more (49% intend to increase spending year-on-year, compared to 36% overall), shop across more product categories (5.4 vs 4.3 average) and are more likely to self-gift (83% vs 67%).”

There’s also insight into how shoppers use messaging apps, and what they’re looking for in brand DMs.

Based on these insights, Meta advised marketers to invest in discovery on social platforms, and to use customer endorsements and testimonials to assure potential customers of their quality.

Meta also said that marketers should design their campaigns for cross-category shoppers: “Use consistent creative systems and shoppable catalogues to reduce the friction between ‘that looks interesting’ and ‘I'm buying this’.”

These notes could help to refine holiday campaign approaches.

#7258. Director of Technology Partnerships at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We’re looking for a Director of Technology Partnerships to lead the teams responsible for growing Supabase through technology integrations and our marketplace ecosystem.

You’ll bring together two complementary motions: partnerships that embed Supabase into the products developers already use, and a marketplace that helps developers discover and connect complementary technologies to their Supabase projects. Your job is to turn both into durable sources of revenue, adoption, and customer value.

Reporting to the Head of Partnerships, you’ll lead and develop the Integrations and Marketplace teams, set their commercial strategy, and work hands-on with our most important partners. A central part of the role is working closely with AI labs to build strategic relationships, develop integrations, and bring joint opportunities to market. You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.

This role is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, where you’ll build relationships with leading AI, developer tools, and infrastructure companies. Supabase is remote-first, and you’ll work across a globally distributed team.

Lead, coach, and develop the Integrations and Marketplace partnerships teams, including team leads and partner managers.

Set a clear strategy for where Supabase invests across strategic technology partnerships, marketplace categories, and emerging ecosystem opportunities.

Define team objectives, partner coverage, investment priorities, and operating cadence. Make thoughtful tradeoffs between high-touch strategic partnerships and scalable programs.

Build a culture of ownership, commercial discipline, and strong cross-functional execution.

Drive revenue from technology integrations through partner-driven customer acquisition, product consumption, expansion, retention, co-sell opportunities, and commercial arrangements.

Own the commercial performance of the technology partnerships and marketplace portfolio, including forecasting and reporting on progress, risks, and return on investment.

Build and deepen relationships with AI labs, working closely with their product, engineering, business development, and executive teams to identify and execute high-impact partnership opportunities.

Develop executive relationships with strategic partners across developer tools, cloud, and adjacent infrastructure.

Lead or support negotiations for complex partnerships, including integration, referral, revenue-sharing, and joint go-to-market agreements.

Help partner managers build joint business plans that connect partner priorities to measurable outcomes for Supabase and its customers.

Lead and develop the Marketplace team, setting its commercial and partner strategy and holding the team accountable for outcomes.

Guide the team in identifying the capabilities developers need, recruiting the right partners, and helping those partners launch and grow.

Set priorities and allocate resources across strategic, high-touch partners and scalable paths for emerging and self-serve partners.

Ensure the team works effectively with Product and Engineering on integration quality, partner onboarding, discovery, activation, and the developer experience across product surfaces.

Enable the team to work with Marketing and Sales to launch integrations, enable teams, and drive ongoing adoption—not just announcements.

Establish clear measures for partner-sourced and influenced pipeline, integration adoption, revenue, consumption, retention, and marketplace performance.

Work with Finance, Data, and Partner Operations to improve attribution, reporting, forecasting, and partner revenue processes.

Represent the voice of partners and customers in product and go-to-market planning, while aligning stakeholders around shared priorities.

Identify risks early, remove blockers, and communicate decisions and outcomes clearly to leadership.

Have significant experience in technology partnerships, business development, or ecosystem leadership at a developer tools, cloud, infrastructure, or SaaS company.

Have led and developed partner-facing teams, including managers or senior individual contributors, and can balance strategic direction with hands-on execution.

Have a track record of building partnerships that produced measurable revenue, product adoption, or customer growth.

Have negotiated complex commercial agreements and understand partnership economics, including revenue share, referrals, and consumption-based models.

Have worked closely with Product and Engineering to ship and grow technical integrations. You can engage credibly with technical teams, including those at AI labs, even if you aren’t the person writing the code.

Know how to build relationships with executives while earning the trust of product, engineering, and go-to-market teams.

Use data to prioritize opportunities, assess partner performance, and make decisions when attribution is imperfect.

Are comfortable building in an evolving environment, communicating in writing, and working asynchronously across time zones.

Built or scaled a developer marketplace, integration ecosystem, or partner platform.

Worked with AI LLMs, AI app builders, databases, open-source products, or developer infrastructure.

A background in software development, with an understanding of how developers build and integrate products.

Experience growing both a small number of strategic partnerships and a broader, scalable partner program.

A strong network in the San Francisco Bay Area technology ecosystem.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.

#7257. Intuit offloads Mailchimp to Bending Spoons to deepen bets on AI

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Bending Spoons, a technology conglomerate whose portfolio includes AOL and Eventbrite, will acquire the email automation company for $3.68 billion.

Intuit has entered into an agreement to sell email automation business Mailchimp to technology conglomerate Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, the company confirmed in its latest earnings report. Intuit acquired Mailchimp in 2021 for $12 billion.

Intuit’s decision to sell comes as Mailchimp continues to be a drag on its business, which includes financial services QuickBooks, TurboTax and Credit Karma. The move is also positioned as a way to sharpen Intuit's focus on artificial intelligence and its other core products.

“We have built AI-native experiences to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline and help them grow through our lead-to-cash capabilities,” said Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit, on a call discussing the company’s latest earnings. “Selling Mailchimp sharpens our focus behind that strategy, while positioning Mailchimp and its team for continued success in their next chapter with Bending Spoons.”

Mailchimp, founded in 2001, was once the gem of the email marketing industry, but in the years following its acquisition by Intuit has struggled to maintain growth. Mailchimp’s revenue decreased 1% to $313 million during Q1 of the company’s fiscal 2027 for the period ended Oct. 31, a contrast to Intuit's overall revenue growth of 12% over the same period.

In May, Intuit announced that it was reducing its full-time workforce by 17% and “rightsizing” its investment in Mailchimp. As struggles persisted, the company in August revealed that it started running Mailchimp as a separate operating segment, a move that was intended to offer investors more transparency as Intuit tried to manage the unit for profitability.

The Mailchimp deal is expected to close in early 2027, at which point Bending Spoons plans to invest “substantially” in Mailchimp and build on its existing tools, according to a separate statement. Bending Spoons, an Italian company founded in 2013, acquires businesses and works to improve them with the goal of keeping them long-term. Other businesses acquired by the company include Vimeo, WeTransfer, Eventbrite, Streamyard and AOL.

Bending Spoons went public in July at a value of over $18 billion. Holding company Berkshire Hathaway commands a 4% ownership stake of the company.

Intuit last week launched a campaign — its first work with agency Mother New York — promoting the integration of its Intuit Intelligence agentic platform into QuickBooks. The campaign, “More Brains for your Business,” positions the AI capabilities as a helping hand instead of a replacement for human talent.
